court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division
holding_summary: A landlord who represents that a furnished house has been put in perfect order, but conceals a leaking roof and a defective cesspool discoverable only in use, commits fraud that lets the tenant avoid rent liability notwithstanding the general rule that a lessor makes no implied covenant to repair or represent premises as tenantable. The court treats the fact that a house was let furnished, ready for occupancy, as a circumstance bearing on whether misrepresentation/deceit occurred.

quotes.text: There is a distinction between letting an unfurnished house and one furnished ready for occupancy, and where the tenant claims misrepresentation and deceit, the fact that the house was let furnished is a circumstance to be considered in determining the question of fact.

While the law of this State undoubtedly is that there is no implied covenant on the part of the lessor to repair, and no implied representation that the premises are tenantable (Franklin v. Brown, 118 N. Y. 110; Daly v. Wise, 132 id. 306), that rule has no application where there is fraudulent misrepresentation or concealment.
